citations.quote:
Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.
If $C$ is at most countable and $m\in\mathbb N$, then the finite product $C^m=\prod_{i<m}C$ is at most countable.

derivations.claim: Define $e:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$ by $e(2n)=n$ and $e(2n+1)=-(n+1)$. Every natural number is uniquely even or odd, and every integer is either a natural number or the negative of a positive natural number; these two descriptions show that every integer is a value of $e$. Thus $e$ is a surjection.
Since $\mathbb{Z}$ is nonempty, [F2] applied to $e$ shows that $\mathbb{Z}$ is at most countable in the sense of [F1].
Since $d$ is finite and positive, [F3] with $C=\mathbb{Z}$ and $m=d$ gives that $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ is at most countable.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the triangle inequality follows from $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$.

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

derivations.claim: Under [F1], $T\mapsto T\otimes I$ preserves products and adjoints because $(T\otimes I)(S\otimes I)=TS\otimes I$ and $(T\otimes I)^*=T^*\otimes I$; it sends $I_\Lambda$ to $I_{\Lambda'}$. The configuration-basis factorization is associative, so for nested regions the two successive inclusions and the direct inclusion act identically on every configuration basis vector and hence are equal operators.

Let $K=\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, and choose its finite orthonormal configuration basis $e_1,\ldots,e_s$. Every $\xi\in\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes K$ has a unique expansion $\xi=\sum_{j=1}^s \xi_j\otimes e_j$, with $\|\xi\|^2=\sum_j\|\xi_j\|^2$. Therefore $\|(T\otimes I)\xi\|^2=\sum_j\|T\xi_j\|^2\le\|T\|^2\|\xi\|^2$, so $\|T\otimes I\|\le\|T\|$.

If $T=0$, both norms are zero. Otherwise, for every $\varepsilon>0$ the supremum definition in [F2] gives a unit vector $u\in\mathcal H_\Lambda$ with $\|Tu\|>\|T\|-\varepsilon$. Since $q\ge1$, $K$ is nonzero; choose a unit configuration vector $v\in K$. Then $\|(T\otimes I)(u\otimes v)\|=\|Tu\|\|v\|>\|T\|-\varepsilon$, so $\|T\otimes I\|\ge\|T\|-\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in step 1.3 and combining with step 1.2 gives $\|\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}(T)\|=\|T\|$. Step 1.1 supplies the unital $*$-homomorphism and composition identities, completing the claim.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a normed space. A **completion of $X$** is a pair
$\bigl(\widehat X,\iota\bigr)$ such that

- $\widehat X$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]);
- $\iota:X\to \widehat X$ is a linear isometry
  ([[def-linear-isometry-and-isometric-isomorphism]]);
- $\iota[X]$ is dense in $\widehat X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

Equivalently, a completion of a normed space is a completion of its norm metric
([[def-metric-completion]]) together with compatible linear structure on the
complete space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space. The published metric completion of the norm metric on $X$ admits
a unique vector-space structure and norm whose induced metric is the
published completion metric and such that the constant sequence embedding
$i:X\to \widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry. With this structure,
$\widehat X$ is a Banach space.

In the published Cauchy-sequence model of the metric completion of a normed
space, if $[x_n]$ and $[y_n]$ denote equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences,
then

$$[x_n]+[y_n]:=[x_n+y_n],\qquad \lambda[x_n]:=[\lambda x_n],\qquad \|[x_n]\|:=\lim_n \|x_n\|$$

are well defined.

A **possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra** is a complex vector space $A$
equipped with an associative complex-bilinear multiplication
$A \times A \to A$ ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]] for the bilinearity convention)
and a norm under which $A$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]],
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]), such that the norm is
**submultiplicative**:

$$\|ab\| \le \|a\|\,\|b\| \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

No multiplicative identity is assumed, and no real-algebra or unital
convention is imported from elsewhere.

A **complex C\*-algebra** is a possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra $A$
equipped with an **involution** $A \to A$, $a \mapsto a^*$, which is
conjugate-linear ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) and
satisfies

$$(a^*)^* = a, \qquad (ab)^* = b^*a^*, \qquad \|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2 \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

The last identity is the **C\*-identity**. Two immediate consequences are worth
recording, and both are proved from the displayed axioms alone:

- **the involution is isometric**: $\|a^*\| = \|a\|$. Indeed $\|a\|^2 = \|a^*a\| \le \|a^*\|\,\|a\|$ gives $\|a\| \le \|a^*\|$ when $a \ne 0$, and applying this inequality to $a^*$ and using $(a^*)^* = a$ gives $\|a^*\| \le \|a\|$; the case $a = 0$ is trivial;
- **no norm-uniqueness assertion is part of this definition**: such a theorem
  needs additional hypotheses and proof, and does not follow merely by naming
  the displayed C\*-identity.

Let $A$ and $B$ be complex C\*-algebras. A **bounded star-homomorphism**, or
bounded $*$-homomorphism, is a bounded complex-linear map
$\varphi : A \to B$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) satisfying

$$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b), \qquad \varphi(a^*) = \varphi(a)^* \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

A star-homomorphism is **not** required to be unital, and it is not required
that a unit be present or preserved; when $A$ and $B$ both happen to be unital,
$\varphi$ is called **unital** if $\varphi(1_A) = 1_B$. The bounded nonunital
star-homomorphisms are the arrows of the locally compact duality theorem on this
page ([[thm-locally-compact-gelfand-duality]]), with properness imposed there
through [[def-approximate-unit-and-proper-c-star-morphism]].

Thus their sum, product and adjoint are defined in a common finite matrix algebra, so $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is a unital $*$-algebra. If $A$ has two localization regions, embedding into their union and isometry [F1] show that both assigned norms equal its norm in that common algebra; hence the local norm is well defined.

By [F3] and [F4], the norm completion is a Banach space and sums, scalar multiples and the limit norm are well defined on Cauchy-sequence classes; the constant sequence at the local unit is its candidate unit, and the local algebra is dense by the definition of completion.

In any common finite matrix algebra, the operator norm is submultiplicative, the adjoint preserves norm, and [F2] supplies the C*-identity $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$. Isometric inclusions [F1] transfer these identities to $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$, so it is a normed $*$-algebra with the C*-identity.

Let $(A_n)$ and $(B_n)$ be Cauchy sequences in $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Each is bounded: after some index its terms lie within one unit of a fixed term, and the finitely many earlier terms have a finite maximum norm. Then
$$\|A_nB_n-A_mB_m\|\le\|A_n\|\,\|B_n-B_m\|+\|A_n-A_m\|\,\|B_m\|$$
shows that $(A_nB_n)$ is Cauchy. If either sequence is replaced by an equivalent one, the same estimate makes the product sequences equivalent. Thus multiplication $[A_n][B_n]:=[A_nB_n]$ is well defined on the completion and obeys $\|xy\|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$.

Since $\|A_n^*-A_m^*\|=\|A_n-A_m\|$ in the local algebra by step 2.1, $[A_n]^*:=[A_n^*]$ is a well-defined involution on the completion. The Cauchy-sequence identities for product and adjoint show $(xy)^*=y^*x^*$ and associativity; continuity of multiplication and the limit norm pass $\|x^*x\|=\|x\|^2$ from [F2] to every $x$ in the completion. The unit class $[I_{\mathrm{loc}}]$ acts as an identity by termwise multiplication and has norm one by isometry, so $\mathcal A$ satisfies the C*-algebra definition in [F5].

If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ with $\Lambda\cap\Delta=\varnothing$, in $\mathcal A_{\Lambda\cup\Delta}$ they have forms $A_\Lambda\otimes I_\Delta$ and $I_\Lambda\otimes B_\Delta$. Both products equal $A_\Lambda\otimes B_\Delta$, so $AB=BA$. This proves locality for disjoint finite local factors.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}(AT)=0$ for every matrix $A$, taking $A=E_{ji}$ makes each entry $T_{ij}$ zero. Hence $\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(I_\Lambda\otimes I_\Delta)=q^rI_\Lambda$. Since $|\Lambda'|=|\Lambda|+r$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(\rho_{\Lambda'})=q^{-|\Lambda'|}q^rI_\Lambda=q^{-|\Lambda|}I_\Lambda=\rho_\Lambda.$$
Thus the family is consistent for every inclusion, including equality of regions ($r=0$).

By [F3], this family extends to a unique algebraic state $\omega$ on $\mathcal A$, and its local restriction is $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(\rho_\Lambda A)=q^{-|\Lambda|}\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$.

$$\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda\cup\Delta}(A\otimes B)=\sum_{i,j}\langle Ae_i,e_i\rangle\langle Bf_j,f_j\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(A)\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(B).$$
